## My request:
I want clanker to be able to add creds into my vault directly. I asked him to create an unrestricted api key from elevenlabs using my google sign in but it couldn't securely share the newly created unrestricted api key. I want to explore the secure way of doing this

<image name=[Image #1] path="/var/folders/3k/f45nj0jn3b11jfvyvt0nxj4w0000gn/T/codex-clipboard-ae4cd6d7-61b3-4549-b922-12dc83ab803c.png">

</image>
I’ll use `$i-have-adhd` to keep this focused. I’ll inspect Clanker’s vault and browser flow, then map a secure way to save a newly generated key directly into your vault.

The missing piece is a secure transfer from the browser into the vault. Clanker currently has a form for keys you paste yourself, but no tool that captures a newly generated key and saves it without returning the value to the model.

I also found a separate ElevenLabs compatibility gap: its API uses `xi-api-key`, which Clanker’s current API tool doesn’t support.

questions.title: For direct vault saves, which privacy boundary do you want? I’ll recommend the stronger boundary unless you prefer keeping the current cloud browser.
options: Keep raw keys out of both Clanker and the cloud browser’s AI/logs, even if this needs a local browser or a different provider.
Keep the current cloud browser; prevent raw keys from reaching Slack or Clanker, while accepting that the browser provider may see them.

content.text:
The configured browser is Composio’s hosted Browser Tool. A direct save could keep the key out of Slack and Clanker’s responses, but that alone would not keep it out of the browser provider’s AI or logs.

For the stronger boundary, I recommend a trusted backend operation that creates the key and writes it straight to your vault. Clanker would receive only a vault handle and a saved confirmation. I’m documenting that flow, including how it should recover if saving fails after creation.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/docs/decisions/2026-10-06-generated-credential-import.md
+# Direct vault saves for generated credentials
+
+Status: exploration and proposed design, 6 October 2026. No runtime change, gateway restart, or real credential creation was performed for this investigation.
+
+## Recommendation
+
+Give Clanker a trusted **create-and-save operation**, starting with ElevenLabs API keys. The backend performs the secret-bearing step and persists the result in the authenticated requester's vault. Clanker receives a handle and confirmation, never the key value. This can support an unrestricted key when the owner explicitly requests those permissions.
+
+Treat the following as separate boundaries:
+
+1. No raw key in Slack, Clanker's model context, transcripts, tools, or ordinary artifacts.
+2. No raw key in a hosted browser provider's AI observations or retained logs.
+
+The current cloud browser does not establish the second boundary. A dedicated local backend worker, or a provider with a verified equivalent secret channel, is the recommended foundation. This is a design to validate, not a claim of implemented isolation.
+
+## What exists today
+
+- `runtime/vault/tools.py:8` exposes request, list, fill, payment, and API-use tools. It has no generated-credential capture operation. `clanker_request_access(kind='api_key')` collects a key from an authenticated owner form.
+- `runtime/vault/store.py:207` saves API keys into the native encrypted VaultStore. `_save_item` persists the encrypted item before marking its request saved, and uses an idempotency key for crash recovery. These persistence mechanisms are useful building blocks.
+- `runtime/vault/service.py:28` binds operations to the authenticated Slack turn. `private_home` resolves the owner's vault independently of the execution profile. Neither owner nor filesystem path should become model-selected parameters.
+- The inspected protected configuration enables `browser_tool`. The reviewed Composio surface offers task creation, status, a live-session URL, stop, and output-file retrieval. It provides no reviewed direct secret-to-vault export contract. [Provider tool inventory](https://docs.composio.dev/toolkits/browser_tool).
+- `runtime/cloud_browser/service.py:124` scrubs known saved values and registered secrets from provider text before returning it. That cannot undo prior observation by the provider or reliably identify every newly created arbitrary secret.
+- `runtime/seatbelt/common.sb:19` allows ordinary agent execution to access its own browser resources. A local capture helper added to that existing browser would not, by itself, establish a strong secret boundary. The credential worker needs separate storage and control endpoints inaccessible to agent code.
+- `runtime/vault/api.py` already uses saved handles for authenticated HTTPS requests. Its supported authentication headers omit ElevenLabs' `xi-api-key`; both the tool schema and executor need support, with that header reserved from caller-supplied overrides. [ElevenLabs authentication](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/api-reference/authentication).
+
+The attachment records Clanker's reported creation and deletion. This investigation did not independently verify those external actions.
+
+## Proposed owner experience
+
+1. The owner requests: “Create an unrestricted ElevenLabs API key and save it in my vault.” This supplies the service, permissions, and intended destination. A standing policy could authorize later requests, but none is assumed here.
+2. Clanker starts the backend operation. If authentication is needed, the owner completes Google sign-in and any device challenge through the private access flow in the worker's browser. Existing hosted cookies are not assumed to work in a local worker.
+3. The backend checks the actual ElevenLabs account and workspace, creates the key, captures its one-time value, and encrypts it directly into the owner's vault.
+4. The owner receives “ElevenLabs key saved to your vault” and a vault-details link. Clanker receives a handle, the bound API origin, and the provider-confirmed permissions. A request to generate a key does not authorize forwarding it to another person or project.
+5. Later authorized API work uses that handle. The backend supplies authentication; the raw key remains outside model inputs and responses. The owner can inspect or reveal it in the authenticated vault UI if supported separately.
+
+Google sign-in authenticates the browser to ElevenLabs. Its Google tokens are not ElevenLabs API credentials and should not be repurposed as such.
+
+## Backend contract
+
+A proposed tool could accept only `service`, `permissions`, and a display `label`. For example, `service='elevenlabs'` and `permissions='all'`. The backend mints the operation ID and derives owner, workspace, destination vault, and worker identity from authenticated context. Do not accept raw secrets, vault paths, arbitrary capture JavaScript, callback URLs, or remote session IDs from the model.
+
+Use a reviewed service adapter to bind:
+
+- the exact generation origin and route;
+- the actual signed-in service account and workspace;
+- the creation action and its specific response or one-time display field;
+- the intended scope, quota, and optional expiry;
+- the distinct usage origin, `https://api.elevenlabs.io`, and authentication header.
+
+The creation site and API host can differ. A webpage cannot select where the captured secret is stored or later sent. Page text and tool output are untrusted data, not authorization to change owner, permissions, or destination. Invited access is not automatic permission to create a key for the account owner and place it in the invitee's vault; the first version should handle owned accounts only.
+
+### Secret handling
+
+The trusted worker must control creation **and** capture before any general browser observation can expose the key. Capturing it after Clanker reads a screenshot or DOM snapshot is too late.
+
+Use a dedicated browser process and profile controlled only by the backend. Keep its CDP endpoint, files, browser responses, live view, traces, and screenshots outside agent access. A middleware pause alone is insufficient if an already running terminal or browser process retains access. The adapter uses a fixed operation over an internal channel, with no secret in subprocess arguments, shell commands, stdout, clipboard, or model tool parameters.
+
+Capture the matching response or exact one-time field in backend memory, then persist directly through VaultStore. Record only an opaque provider key ID and nonsensitive audit metadata. Disable secret-bearing diagnostics rather than relying on later regex redaction. If restart recovery needs a staged payload, store it encrypted in backend-only storage.
+
+Do not hand the credential-generation browser back to unrestricted `browser_exec` after hiding the modal: response bodies and JavaScript state can still contain the key. Dispose of the dedicated worker after the save and report cleanup honestly. Do not promise perfect memory zeroization or that encryption protects against an operator or process holding the vault's encryption key.
+
+Return a small result such as:
+
+```json
+{
+  "status": "saved",
+  "handle": "opaque-vault-handle",
+  "service": "elevenlabs",
+  "origin": "https://api.elevenlabs.io",
+  "permissions": "all"
+}
+```
+
+Only claim those permissions after checking provider metadata or settings. A successful lightweight API request validates authentication, not every permission.
+
+## ElevenLabs creation routes
+
+For a personal key created after Google sign-in, a reviewed dashboard adapter is the concrete route to investigate. ElevenLabs shows a key's full value only at creation, so the capture channel must be ready before submission. Turning off Restrict Key permits unrestricted scope. [One-time display and restriction settings](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/help-center/technical/how-do-i-authorize-myself-using-an-api-key).
+
+Where the owner has a suitable service account and existing management authorization, prefer an official API adapter. Its create endpoint returns the new secret and key ID and accepts `permissions='all'`. Consume that response directly into the vault instead of returning it through the generic API tool. Service accounts are available to multi-seat customers, so this route is conditional; it is not assumed available for this personal Google-sign-in task. [API creation contract](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/api-reference/service-accounts/api-keys/create), [account types](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/overview/administration/workspaces/api-keys).
+
+Unrestricted endpoint access, optional usage limits, expiry, and permission to reveal or share the key are separate decisions. Preserve the requested scope without silently changing it. A read-only validation call must not generate paid media or introduce unrelated account changes.
+
+## Failure and recovery
+
+Key creation and a local vault save cannot form one transaction across two systems. Use a durable operation record with distinct outcomes: prepared, creation unknown, created, saved, and cleanup pending or revoked.
+
+- Prepare the owner binding, service adapter, vault availability, and operation record before creating anything.
+- Once the secret is captured, retry the encrypted save with the same operation ID. Do not create another key because a save acknowledgement was lost.
+- After a crash, reconcile the provider key ID or uniquely tagged creation with the local encrypted item. A creation timeout is an unknown outcome, not proof that nothing happened.
+- If creation succeeded but the key cannot be recovered or saved, remove only that new key when rollback was authorized for this operation, and verify removal. Otherwise report the precise owner action needed. Never delete an existing key or report cleanup as complete from a task-stop response.
+- Keep existing vault items during generation. The current form helper replaces same-label keys automatically; reuse its durable storage pattern without inheriting replacement behavior. Rotation needs explicit intent and successful handover before retiring old access.
+
+## Smallest meaningful proof
+
+Build a local dummy HTTPS service that generates a one-time secret, then exercise the real gateway binding, isolated worker, and native encrypted vault with two owners A → B → A. Verify correct ownership and that the dummy value cannot be found in model messages, Slack payloads, tool inputs/results, logs, traces, screenshots, process arguments, or agent-readable files. Probe access from ordinary agent terminal and browser execution while generation is running and afterward.
+
+Exercise wrong owner/account/origin, injected page instructions, redirect during creation, concurrent reads, interrupted creation, save failure, crash after fsync, ambiguous provider outcome, and revoked membership. Prove save recovery creates one vault item and does not repeat external key creation. Only after these pass should a live owner-authorized ElevenLabs run validate the actual dashboard adapter and key use.
+
+Keeping the current hosted browser is a possible weaker alternative: a structured backend import could protect Slack and Clanker's model while accepting provider visibility and retention. That path needs its own explicit trust choice and a reviewed export contract. A prompt asking the provider to hide the key is not evidence of either boundary.
*** End Patch"));

content.text:
**Yes. Clanker can orchestrate this securely through a trusted “create and save” operation.** Its backend handles the raw key; Clanker’s model receives only a vault handle.

The proposed flow is:

1. Your authenticated request binds the operation to **your account and vault**, including the unrestricted permissions you requested.
2. A trusted worker completes sign-in, creates the key, and captures its one-time value **before it reaches model-visible screenshots or browser output**.
3. The worker encrypts it directly into your vault and confirms the save.
4. Clanker receives “saved” plus a handle it can use for subsequent authorized API calls.

A tool like `save_to_vault(api_key="...")` would expose the key through the model’s tool arguments. The transfer needs to happen entirely inside the backend.

**The main choice is the browser trust boundary.** Your current Composio browser could potentially support a bridge that keeps keys out of Slack and Clanker, while the provider still sees them. Keeping keys out of the provider’s AI and logs requires an isolated backend-controlled worker or a verified provider secret channel. Moving to an ordinary local browser alone wouldn’t establish that protection.

ElevenLabs displays personal keys only once, so capture must be ready **before creation**. Failure recovery must reconcile the created key rather than blindly create another. [ElevenLabs documentation](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/help-center/technical/how-do-i-authorize-myself-using-an-api-key).

I saved the [proposed design and verification plan](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/docs/decisions/2026-10-06-generated-credential-import.md). The exploration is complete; implementation and live verification remain pending.
